prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B022, Katori and Ye. Having read all eight first-round statements and the chair's questions, what strengthens my view is that the reasons given are largely independent of each other. Danielsson argues from discovery, Kroll from a new way of observing nature, Eriksson from reproducibility, Pearce from instrument practice, and I from the fact that the physics can be explained with one picture and checked in detail. The picture is a standing wave at the magic wavelength, where the light shift is the same for both clock levels and drops out, while the tight confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects for thousands of atoms at once. The result then rests on atomic structure theory (polarizabilities, blackbody and collisional shifts) that can be tested against experiment, and the 10^-18 level has been reached and compared across several laboratories. The delivered science is more than a figure of merit: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, a many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock regime, and limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. On the chair's question about the citation, I would write both parts: the invention of the lattice clock, which is Katori's magic-wavelength concept and first demonstrations, and its development to 10^-18, which is where Ye's group took it. Writing both keeps the two names matched to the two decisive steps and does not rest the prize on a record number alone. On whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, I say no. That is a decision by metrology bodies about the unit and not a test of the physics, which is already settled by independent reproduction.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot fully remove is lineage. The frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) prizes were also in time and frequency, and a reader may see this as the next increment in one programme. My answer is the citation, which should name the lattice architecture and the magic-wavelength condition explicitly, since those are what neither earlier prize covered. A second point I take seriously, in light of Pearce's and Eriksson's remarks, is that so far the largest scientific returns are upper limits and consistency checks, not a new effect. A prize for an instrument can be read as engineering. I accept that this is a real cost and that a member who weighs discovery of a new phenomenon more heavily than I do can reasonably hold that view. Credit also remains incomplete: Lemonde and SYRTE, Gill, and Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom on the JILA side contributed, and I cannot verify priority from the packet. I still do not think this breaks a two-name award, but I would not claim it is free of doubt.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B022 first, argues that many neutral atoms in a lattice give statistics a single ion cannot match, and accepts that the largest returns (dark matter, constants, geodesy) are still prospective. He also discloses a mild personal link to the B022 community through John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the statistics argument and would put it into the citation, since it is the plain answer to why this is not just the ion-clock prize again. On your disclosure, I read it as a one-step-removed link: a year in a laboratory where a later Ye collaborator was a close colleague, and no work with Katori or Ye. I do not think it needs more than disclosure, and the committee can note it. My own position is similar and I disclose it below. On the prospective returns, I would be less defensive than you are. A millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the Fermi-degenerate clock are already demonstrated results, not promises, and the citation can say 'a new regime of precision' without claiming a discovery that has not been made.

responses.point: Pearce notes that the discovery content so far is mostly upper limits and consistency tests with no new effect observed, and that Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team.
responses.response: Both points are fair. On the first, I would distinguish between a discovery of a new effect and a discovery of a new regime. Nobody had seen that an optical clock could be run with thousands of atoms in a lattice at 10^-18 with all shifts under control, and that is a result in itself, even if the dark-matter and constants searches only set limits. On the second, the Nobel statutes allow us to credit the person who led the decisive step. Ye led the JILA programme that established the record regime, and Katori made the concept and first demonstrations. If you consider that Ye's contribution is better described as the leadership of a systematic programme than as a single idea, I would accept a citation wording that says 'development' and not 'discovery', which fits the facts. I do not think the team size is a reason to add names, because I cannot name a third person whose contribution matches those two.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes the citation 'for the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new precision tests of nature' and calls B022 a clue pulled out of nature by measurement.
responses.response: I largely agree with your wording and with the framing of a clue pulled out of nature. I would be careful with the phrase 'opening new precision tests of nature', which is a promise about the future, and a committee that is sceptical about the discovery-versus-tool question will read it as one. I prefer to name something already done, for example the magic-wavelength trapping and the 10^-18 level, and let the reader conclude the rest. I would accept your wording if the committee prefers it, but I would not insist on the forward-looking phrase. On your fallback, I rank B020 above B028 as a second choice, but I defer to you on how settled the moire pairing mechanism is.

responses.point: Mehlig, who opened with B011, argues that B022 is persuasive on its own terms and not merely popular, and notes that a second part would need three names and cannot be combined with Katori and Ye under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and the three-person limit is the decisive argument against a second part. Adding any second part with two or more names would force one of Katori or Ye out, and I do not accept that. I also see no candidate on the shortlist whose case is strong enough this year to justify cutting the credit in B022. B020 could be reduced to Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, but only with the Mott-insulator experiment of Greiner included, and then three people would be needed and the configuration would exceed the limit. I therefore hold B020 and B004 as alternatives if B022 does not carry, not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I judge yes, but this is a judgement about prize-level novelty and I cannot prove it.
Priority of Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom relative to Katori and Ye. I have worked from the packet and my own recollection, not from primary documents.
Weight between Katori's concept and Ye's record performance, and therefore whether the citation should lead with 'invention' or with 'development'.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay an award. I think not, but colleagues who disagree are making a defensible argument.
My own limits outside atomic and quantum physics: I defer to colleagues on astroparticle and condensed-matter entries if B022 fails and a fallback has to be chosen.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, unchanged in substance: no specific conflict for B022. My collaborations are with the Lund attosecond group (L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate) and with Keller's group at ETH, and not with the clock groups of Katori or Ye. I am a theorist in atomic, molecular and optical physics and so professionally close to this subfield, but this is shared closeness and not a personal tie. I have no recusal issue for B020 or B004 either, though I note that my storage-ring recombination work is a general neighbour of precision atomic spectroscopy. I take note of Kroll's disclosure through John Hall's laboratory and agree that disclosure is enough.
